1:
Henry begins with the transaction and calls it a good bargain, whatever Potiphar gave, better than the merchandise of silver — and quotes the Jewish proverb that if the world did but know the worth of good men, they would hedge them about with pearls. Wesley repeats that sentence almost word for word, and both go on to the same consolation: his brethren had stripped him of his coat of many colours but could not strip him of his virtue and prudence, and those who can separate us from all our friends cannot deprive us of the gracious presence of our God. Calvin puts the theology under it. It is never well with men except so far as the Lord shows himself gracious to them, for though he vouchsafes his blessing for a time even to reprobates, he meanwhile curses their felicity, so that what they took for the height of fortune turns to ruin. The world forms for itself a goddess of fortune, or else each man adores his own industry, but Scripture teaches that adversity is a sign of God's absence and prosperity of his presence. He adds a caution against reading the verse too grandly: Joseph was not at once elevated, but is reckoned among the slaves and holds his life subject to his master's will, so that we should learn even amid our sufferings to perceive the grace of God, content to have our cup mingled with some portion of sweetness.

What Potiphar saw is treated carefully. Gill grants that the master knew nothing of the spiritual and gracious presence of God and was no judge of it, but perceived by the ingenuity of Joseph's mind, his ready and speedy learning of the Egyptian language, and his dexterity and faithfulness in everything, that here was an extraordinary person for his age. Calvin makes more of the admission, since the grace of God shone out so plainly that it became manifest even to a heathen, blind in this respect — from which he concludes that heathens may be so affected by religion as to be constrained to ascribe glory to God. Yet the man's ingratitude betrays itself at once, for he despises the God whose gifts he estimates so highly in Joseph; he ought at least to have inquired who that God was, and instead deems it enough, so far as it is to his private advantage, to acknowledge that his slave is divinely directed and to use his labour with the greater profit. Clarke notes the office he was given, the Hebrew verb meaning to visit, take care of, superintend, and answering to the Greek word from which we have overseer or bishop.

The chapter's last quiet sentence is where the trouble begins. Wesley, again following Henry, observes that the master knew not aught he had save the bread which he did eat, the servant having all the care and trouble of the estate and the master only the enjoyment of it — an example not to be imitated by any master, unless he could be sure of having a Joseph for his servant. Keil states the turn baldly: Joseph was handsome in form and feature, and Potiphar's wife set her eyes upon the handsome young man. Clarke reports how far that beauty travelled: it is celebrated over all the East, Mohammed devoting a whole chapter of the Koran to him and the Persian poets Jamy and Nizamy each writing a poem on Joseph and Zuleekha, as the Asiatics call Potiphar's wife. Calvin draws the sober moral from the same fact: since elegance of form was the occasion of great calamity to Joseph, let us not greatly desire those graces of person which conciliate the favour of the world, but let each be content with his own lot, seeing how readily Satan turns the gifts of God into snares to catch souls.
7:
Henry traces the beginning of the thing to a look. Her sin began in the eye, and the warning follows at once: remarkable beauty, in men or women, often proves a dangerous snare both to its owner and to others, and we have great need to make a covenant with our eyes lest the eye infect the heart — she had a husband who ought to have been to her a covering of the eyes from all others. What followed he calls daring and shameless, for where the unclean spirit gets dominion in a soul the clothes of modesty are thrown off and the bands of shame broken in pieces, and lust once headstrong will stick at nothing and blush at nothing. Calvin supposes the account compressed, since Moses touches only the chief points and there is no doubt that this impure woman tried various arts upon the pious youth, insinuating herself by indirect blandishments long before she broke out into so shameless a licence.

The refusal is given two reasons, and the voices weigh both. Gill prefers to read the boast the other way — not that Joseph was greater than his fellow servants, but that his master himself was not greater in the house than he, having a larger propriety in it but no larger use of it. Clarke numbers the reasons plainly — gratitude to the master to whom he owed all that he had, and fear of the God in whose sight it would be a heinous offence — and asks how, with the kindness of the one and the displeasure of the other before his eyes, he could have committed an act that would at once have marked him the most ungrateful and the most worthless of men. Calvin finds the finer point in the form of the argument: Joseph acknowledges himself the more strictly bound the greater the power entrusted to him, and ingenuous men have this property, that the more is confided to them the less they can bear to deceive. Nor would he seem restrained only by regard to man, and so he adds that the act would offend God — for nothing is more powerful to overcome temptation than the fear of God. Wesley presses the same last clause hardest: not only how shall I sin against my master, my mistress, myself, my own body and soul, but against God? Gracious souls, he says, look upon this as the worst thing in sin, that it is against God, against his nature and his dominion; and they that love God for this reason hate sin.

What makes the episode remarkable to Henry is that the refusal was repeated. He rates the escape, all things considered, as great an instance of the divine power as the deliverance of the three children out of the fiery furnace, and lists what was ranged against it: the tempter was his mistress, whom it was his place to obey and his interest to oblige, and whose enmity he courted at his peril; and Satan, finding he could not overcome this man with troubles and the frowns of the world, assaulted him instead with soft and charming pleasures, which have slain their ten thousands. Calvin says the constancy shows a real fear of God reigning in him, since he not only repelled one attack but stood forth to the last the conqueror of all; and he notes how easily we fall when Satan tempts us through another, seeming exempt from blame if the one who induces us bears a part of it. Wesley draws the practical rule from the words that he would not so much as be with her: those that would be kept from harm must keep themselves out of harm's way. Keil marks the phrase that turns the story, literally about this day — the day the writer has in mind.
11:
Gill gathers the guesses about the day. It was a week, a month, or rather a year after she first began, as Aben Ezra reckoned; Josephus made it a public festival which the women attended, from which she excused herself by pretending illness, and Jarchi a noted day at the idol's temple. On any of these accounts she knew Joseph would be at home and not there, and judged it a fit opportunity to attack him once more. Gill supposes she seized his garment because he had learned to get away as soon as she began to speak, so that only by holding him could she gain a hearing; Wesley says he would not stay to parley with the temptation but flew from it with the utmost abhorrence, leaving the garment behind him as one escaping for his life. Calvin calls this the crisis of the combat. Joseph had already shown a memorable constancy, a youth tempted through a long succession of days who, at an age to which intemperance is commonly pardoned, was more moderate than almost any old man; but now the woman openly raves, and the more arduous the contest the more worthy of praise is a magnanimity that remains inflexible.

What Joseph stood to lose, Calvin states exactly: he saw that he must incur the danger of losing both his character and his life, chose to sacrifice his character, and was prepared to relinquish life itself rather than be guilty of such wickedness before God. From that Calvin turns on the excuses men make of their reputation — I wish to avoid offence, I am afraid lest men interpret amiss what I have done aright — for no one proves that he heartily loves virtue but he who, content with God as his only witness, does not hesitate to submit to any disgrace rather than decline from the path of duty.

The accusation is the mirror image of the crime, and every voice notices it. Keil puts it plainly: when the daring assault upon his chastity had failed on account of his faithfulness and fear of God, the adulterous woman reversed the whole affair and charged him with an attack upon her modesty, to have her revenge and avert suspicion from herself — and in doing it she does not think her husband worth naming, while a Hebrew man was no ornamental epithet to Egyptian ears. Henry marks the same turn as a change in the passion itself: now her love was turned into the utmost rage and malice, and she pretends she cannot endure the sight of him whom a while ago she could not endure out of her sight, for chaste and holy love will continue though it is slighted, whereas sinful love, like Amnon's to Tamar, is easily changed into sinful hatred. He notices too that she calls her husband neither her husband nor her lord but only he, having forgotten the covenant of her God that was between them, and draws the hard conclusion that innocence itself cannot secure a reputation, since not every one who keeps a good conscience can keep a good name. Clarke reads the same clause as a calculated stroke at a man she did not greatly love — he hath brought in a Hebrew unto us, that is, he raised this person to all his dignity and eminence and so gave him the greater opportunity to mock us — and notes that the word rendered mock is the one used of Isaac and Rebekah, a familiarity allowable only between man and wife. Calvin sees the design behind calling the servants at all: she who had before sought secrecy now summons her domestics, so that by this prejudging of the case she may condemn the youth before ever her husband hears it, and by involving her husband in the charge compel him, for shame, to avenge her.
16:
Gill follows the small deliberate steps by which the charge was built. She laid up the garment beside her as a proof of what she laid to his charge and as a testimony against him, keeping it until her lord came home; and when he came she told him the affair in much the same manner and to the same import as she had told it to the men of the house, so that the two accounts should answer one another. The cry she reports, Gill glosses as she would have it understood — that she lifted up her voice for help from the servants, frightened at an insolent attempt — and he does not let the sentence stand without naming it for what it was: the story she related to her husband was her own invention, and a lie.

That the husband believed it is what the commentators find hardest, and Calvin divides the blame carefully. Seeing that so probable a colour had been given to the transaction, it is no wonder that jealousy, whose motions are exceedingly vehement and ardent, prevailed so far with Potiphar as to make him credit his wife's calumnies. What cannot be excused is the levity with which he instantly thrust into prison a servant he had found prudent and honest, without examining the cause; he ought to have been less under the influence of his wife, and he received the just reward of his too easy folly by cherishing with honour a harlot in the place of a wife. From this Calvin draws a warning for husbands in particular, that they must use prudence lest they be carried rashly hither and thither at the will of their wives; and since we everywhere see that men too obsequious to their wives are held up to ridicule, we should learn to pray for the spirit of gravity and moderation. He also disposes of an objection raised against the story, that Potiphar is called an eunuch and could have felt no jealousy: in the East the word was used not only of those who were so in fact but of satraps and nobles, so that it means here no more than that he was one of the chief men of the court.

What the sentence lacked was any hearing at all. Calvin says Moses expressly condemns the rashness of a man who took fire as soon as he had heard his wife and gave the reins to his indignation just as if the guilt had been proved, since by that course all equity is excluded, no just defence is allowed, and the true and accurate investigation of the cause is utterly rejected. Henry looks at the same silence from Joseph's side and finds two possible reasons, either that he durst not make his defence by telling the truth, since it would have reflected too heavily upon his mistress, or that his master would not hear him or would not believe him; and there was no remedy, for he is condemned to perpetual imprisonment. Yet Henry sees a restraint even in the anger. God held back that wrath, or it would have put Joseph to death, and the wrath which imprisoned him God afterwards made to turn to his praise. He adds two things about the injustice. Many an action of false imprisonment, he says, will in the great day be found to lie against the enemies and persecutors of God's people; and our Lord Jesus, like Joseph here, was bound and numbered with the transgressors.
20:
Gill wonders that the sentence was no worse. As captain of the guard Potiphar had power to imprison of himself, and as chief of the executioners it is much that he did not in his passion hand Joseph over to be put to death at once; perhaps something of his old respect survived the impeachment, or he had heard Joseph's apology before committing him, though for his wife's credit he took this step — or else things were so overruled by the providence of God. Of the place itself Gill notes that the Hebrew word carries the sense of roundness and may be rendered the round house or round tower, and Clarke agrees the prison was probably built in that form. Wesley, following Henry, thinks Potiphar chose this prison because it was the worst, for there the irons entered into the soul; but God designed it to pave the way to Joseph's enlargement. Calvin agrees that the beginning was severe, since Moses does not say how Joseph was afflicted at first but we readily gather that he was allowed no liberty and thrust into some obscure dungeon: the keeper was under Potiphar's power and at his disposal, and what clemency could be hoped from a man jealous and carried away with the vehemence of his anger?

The turn in the prison is credited by all of them to God rather than to Joseph's merits. Keil describes the arrangement precisely — the keeper was the governor of the prison, himself under Potiphar as captain of the guard, and it was Jehovah who procured Joseph favour in his eyes, so that he entrusted all the prisoners to his care. Calvin insists on the sequence: the Lord purposely suffered Joseph to be reduced to extremity, that he might bring him back as from the grave, for as the light of the sun is most clearly seen when we look out from a dark place, so in the darkness of our miseries the grace of God shines more brightly. That the keeper became humane at all he ascribes to a mind not spontaneously disposed to equity being divinely inclined to it, since God governs the hearts of men according to his will. Wesley puts it shorter: God despises not his prisoners, and can raise up friends for them where they little expect any. Gill measures the trust by what the keeper stopped doing: he did not inquire into or examine the management, nor take any account of what was in Joseph's hands — the Targums paraphrasing the clause to mean that he saw no crime in him.

Calvin raises the question the narrative leaves open, why the keeper did not fear Potiphar's displeasure, and why Potiphar, who could easily have interfered, allowed a man he mortally hated to be treated so kindly and liberally. His cruelty may have been divinely restrained; but Calvin thinks it also probable that Potiphar had come to suspect his wife's subtle scheme, and that though appeased towards Joseph he was unwilling to acquit him to his own dishonour. What Calvin admires most comes last: when Joseph is made guard of the prison and has the free administration of it, he nevertheless makes no attempt to escape, but waits for the proper season of his liberation. Clarke closes the chapter with two reflections of his own. It is of little consequence where the lot of a servant of God may be cast, since like Joseph he is ever employed for his master and God prospers his work; and a woman of that spirit is capable of any evil, for when she could not get her wicked ends answered she began to accuse — which is precisely Satan's custom, who first tempts men to sin and then charges them with having committed it, even where the temptation has been faithfully and perseveringly resisted.
